pos: adv. (in mourning; in Malachi, the complaint of men who had walked mournfully and thought God owed them for it)
etymology: From Old English murnan, to grieve. At Malachi 3:14 it renders a Hebrew word meaning in black or in mourning garb — the outward dress of penitence, worn as a claim.
biblical_def:
Malachi records what the people were saying about God behind His back, and it is a grievance: Ye have said, It is vain to serve God: and what profit is it that we have kept his ordinance, and that we have walked mournfully before the LORD of hosts? They had kept the ordinance. They had walked in mourning dress. And they had worked out that it had not paid. The LORD's answer opens the paragraph — Your words have been stout against me — and He will not let them pretend they said nothing: Yet ye say, What have we spoken so much against thee?

Isaiah records the same complaint almost word for word: Wherefore have we fasted, say they, and thou seest not? wherefore have we afflicted our soul, and thou takest no knowledge? And God answers with the facts of their behaviour — in the day of your fast ye find pleasure and exact all your labours. Mourning worn as a device is not mourning. But the passage in Malachi does not end with the rebuke, and what follows is one of the most tender verses in the prophets. Then they that feared the LORD spake often one to another: and the LORD hearkened, and heard it, and a book of remembrance was written before him. In the same congregation, at the same hour, some were computing what religion owed them and others were talking about God to each other, and He was listening to both.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): in a mournful manner; with sorrow; with an appearance of grief.
webster_full: MOURNFULLY, adv. In a mournful manner; with sorrow; with grief; so as to express sorrow.
MOURN, v.i. To grieve; to lament; to sorrow; to wear the customary habit of sorrow.
SACKCLOTH, n. Cloth of which sacks are made; coarse cloth worn in mourning or in penitence.
ORDINANCE, n. A rule established by authority; a permanent rule of action; an established rite or ceremony.
PROFIT, n. Gain; advantage; any accession of good from labor or exertion.
scriptures: Malachi 3:14
Ye have said, It is vain to serve God: and what profit is it that we have kept his ordinance, and that we have walked mournfully before the LORD of hosts?
Malachi 3:13
Your words have been stout against me, saith the LORD. Yet ye say, What have we spoken so much against thee?
Isaiah 58:3

Wherefore have we fasted, say they, and thou seest not? wherefore have we afflicted our soul, and thou takest no knowledge? Behold, in the day of your fast ye find pleasure, and exact all your labours.
Malachi 3:16

Then they that feared the LORD spake often one to another: and the LORD hearkened, and heard it, and a book of remembrance was written before him for them that feared the LORD, and that thought upon his name.
corruption_summary: Religious observance is performed as a claim on God, and when the claim is not honoured the worshipper concludes that serving God is vain — the exact sentence Malachi records.
corruption_paragraphs: It is vain to serve God is the conclusion of a transaction that did not settle as expected, and the transaction had to exist first. These men had kept ordinances and worn mourning as payments, and the grievance is the receipt. The same logic runs through the prosperity teaching, but also through much quieter religion: a believer who has attended faithfully, given consistently, and suffered anyway, and who finds a complaint rising that he cannot quite name. Malachi is worth reading at that moment, not to shame him but to show him what the complaint actually is — words stout against God, spoken by men who genuinely did not think they had said anything.

The corrective is the verse that follows, and it names a different way of being religious in the same room. They that feared the LORD spake often one to another — not computing, not appealing, simply talking about Him — and He hearkened, and heard, and wrote it down. The distinguishing mark is not the amount of observance but whether God is the end of it or the means. They shall be mine, saith the LORD of hosts, in that day when I make up my jewels, which is the only profit the fearing ones were ever after.

pos: n. (sorrow of countenance; which Ecclesiastes says makes the heart better)
etymology: From Old English saed, sated or weary. At Ecclesiastes 7:3 it renders Hebrew roa panim, literally badness of face — a face gone heavy.
biblical_def:
Ecclesiastes states a thing nobody wants to hear and states it flatly: Sorrow is better than laughter: for by the sadness of the countenance the heart is made better. The Hebrew is literally the badness of the face — a countenance gone heavy — and the verse claims that a heavy face does something to a heart that a light one does not. The surrounding verses press the point: It is better to go to the house of mourning, than to go to the house of feasting: for that is the end of all men; and the living will lay it to his heart, and The heart of the wise is in the house of mourning; but the heart of fools is in the house of mirth.

The claim is not that gloom is godly. Ecclesiastes elsewhere commends bread eaten with joy and a garment always white. The claim is that a funeral tells the truth about the human situation and a party does not, and that a man who has stood at a graveside and laid it to his heart is in a better position to live than a man who has arranged never to go. Paul sharpens the distinction the New Testament makes on the whole subject: godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation not to be repented of: but the sorrow of the world worketh death. Two sorrows, and they look identical from outside. One drives a man to God, and the other drives him further in on himself.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): sorrowfulness; mournfulness; dejection of mind; gravity of countenance.
webster_full: SADNESS, n. Sorrowfulness; mournfulness; dejection of mind; also, seriousness; gravity.
SAD, a. Sorrowful; affected with grief; cast down; also, serious; grave; not gay or volatile.
MOURNING, n. The act of sorrowing or expressing grief; lamentation; the dress or customary habit worn by mourners.
COUNTENANCE, n. The whole form of the face; the system of features; the face; aspect; look.
GRAVE, a. Of weighty character; serious; sober; solemn; not light, trifling or jocose.

Ecclesiastes 7:2
It is better to go to the house of mourning, than to go to the house of feasting: for that is the end of all men; and the living will lay it to his heart.
2 Corinthians 7:10
For godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation not to be repented of: but the sorrow of the world worketh death.
Nehemiah 2:2
Wherefore the king said unto me, Why is thy countenance sad, seeing thou art not sick? this is nothing else but sorrow of heart. Then I was very sore afraid,
corruption_summary: Sadness is treated as a malfunction to be eliminated, and a church shaped by that assumption has nothing to say at a graveside and nothing to do with Ecclesiastes 7.
corruption_paragraphs: The prevailing assumption is that sorrow is a problem, and the only question is which method removes it. Ecclesiastes says something no modern discourse will say: that sorrow is better than laughter, and that a heavy face improves a heart. The Bible is not romanticizing misery; it is observing that grief teaches what comfort cannot, that the house of mourning tells the truth about the end of all men, and that the wise deliberately go there. A congregation that has made its gatherings a permanent house of mirth has made itself useless to its own members on the worst day of their lives.

At the same time Scripture refuses to bless all sorrow indiscriminately. Paul's distinction is exact and is the one thing a grieving believer most needs: godly sorrow works repentance, and the sorrow of the world works death. Judas and Peter both wept. One went out and hanged himself and the other was restored by a charcoal fire on a beach. The difference was not the depth of the grief but its direction. Anyone working through his own sadness has one useful question — does this drive me toward God or away from Him? — and Scripture treats the answer as decisive.

pos: n. (misery; Moses' word for what he asked God not to make him watch)
etymology: From Old English wrecca, an exile or outcast. At Numbers 11:15 it renders Hebrew ra'ah, evil or calamity — Moses asking not to see his own.
biblical_def:
Moses has been given a people who weep for flesh, and his prayer is one of the bluntest in the Bible: And if thou deal thus with me, kill me, I pray thee, out of hand, if I have found favour in thy sight; and let me not see my wretchedness. He has already said I am not able to bear all this people alone, because it is too heavy for me, and before that had asked God why the burden was laid on him at all. This is the meekest man in all the earth asking to be killed rather than to go on, and the Holy Ghost preserved it without editing.

What God does with it is the point. There is no rebuke. He tells Moses to gather seventy elders, and says, I will take of the spirit which is upon thee, and will put it upon them; and they shall bear the burden of the people with thee, that thou bear it not thyself alone. The answer to a crushed leader is not a scolding and not a miracle but seventy men. Paul's use of the same word in Romans 7 shows how far it reaches: O wretched man that I am! who shall deliver me from the body of this death? — and there too the cry is answered in the next breath rather than left hanging: I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord. Scripture lets its best men say the worst thing they are feeling, and then answers it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): extreme misery or unhappiness; a state of distress or affliction.
webster_full: WRETCHEDNESS, n. Extreme misery or unhappiness, either from want or from pain of body or anguish of mind.
WRETCH, n. A miserable person; one sunk in vice or degradation; one deeply afflicted.
MISERY, n. Great unhappiness; extreme pain of body or mind; wretchedness; distress.
BURDEN, n. That which is borne or carried; a load; that which is grievous, wearisome or oppressive.
ELDER, n. One who is older; in Scripture, a person who on account of age is selected to be a ruler or officer.
scriptures: Numbers 11:15
And if thou deal thus with me, kill me, I pray thee, out of hand, if I have found favour in thy sight; and let me not see my wretchedness.
Numbers 11:14
I am not able to bear all this people alone, because it is too heavy for me.
Numbers 11:17

And I will come down and talk with thee there: and I will take of the spirit which is upon thee, and will put it upon them; and they shall bear the burden of the people with thee, that thou bear it not thyself alone.
Romans 7:24
O wretched man that I am! who shall deliver me from the body of this death?
corruption_summary: Despair in a believer is met with rebuke or with silence, when Scripture records it from Moses, Elijah, Job, Jeremiah and Paul, and shows God answering rather than scolding.
corruption_paragraphs: A Christian who says what Moses said in Numbers 11 will generally be corrected before he is heard. Yet the Bible preserves the sentence, and preserves Elijah under the juniper asking to die, and Job cursing his day, and Jeremiah wishing he had not been born, and Jonah saying it was better for him to die than to live. In not one of these cases is the man rebuked for the words. Elijah is given sleep and food and then a quiet voice; Job is answered out of the whirlwind and then vindicated; Moses is given seventy men. God's treatment of His exhausted servants is the strongest argument in Scripture against the reflex to hush them.

That does not make despair true. Moses was wrong about his situation, and Paul's O wretched man that I am is followed immediately by I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord. But the order matters, and the church routinely reverses it: the answer is supplied before the cry has been allowed. Numbers 11 shows the better pattern — let the man say it, in full, to God; and then do what God did, which was to lift the actual weight off him by putting other shoulders under it.

pos: n. (the state of being guilty; what Abimelech says Isaac's lie nearly brought upon a whole people)
etymology: From Old English gylt, a crime or fault. At Genesis 26:10 it renders Hebrew asham, guilt — the same noun as the trespass offering, which made objective guilt a thing that could be brought and dealt with.
biblical_def:
Isaac has done in Gerar exactly what his father did twice before — called his wife his sister out of fear — and the pagan king rebukes him: And Abimelech said, What is this thou hast done unto us? one of the people might lightly have lien with thy wife, and thou shouldest have brought guiltiness upon us. Two things in that sentence are worth noticing. The first is who is speaking: a Philistine king has a clearer sense of the danger than the covenant heir does. The second is the grammar of the guilt — it would have been brought upon them, as a thing that arrives and settles, not merely as a feeling anyone would have had.

That objectivity is the Hebrew word's whole point. Asham is guilt as a status before God, and it is the same word used for the trespass offering — because guilt of that kind cannot be talked away but must be carried off by a sacrifice. The law makes this concrete: the man who sinned had to restore what he took, add the fifth part, and bring his ram. Scripture also knows the other side, the guilt that is felt, and David describes what it cost him to keep it in: his bones waxed old, his moisture was turned into the drought of summer, until I acknowledged my sin unto thee, and mine iniquity have I not hid... and thou forgavest the iniquity of my sin. Guilt in the Bible is a fact before it is a feeling, and the remedy addresses the fact.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): the state of being guilty; criminality; guilt; liability to punishment.
webster_full: GUILTINESS, n. The state of being guilty; wickedness; criminality; guilt.
GUILT, n. Criminality; that state of a moral agent which results from his actual commission of a crime.
TRESPASS, n. Any voluntary transgression of the moral law; any violation of a known rule of duty; sin.
RESTITUTION, n. The act of returning or restoring to a person some thing or right of which he has been unjustly deprived.
ACKNOWLEDGE, v.t. To own, avow or admit to be true, by a declaration of assent.

And Abimelech said, What is this thou hast done unto us? one of the people might lightly have lien with thy wife, and thou shouldest have brought guiltiness upon us.
Genesis 26:7

And the men of the place asked him of his wife; and he said, She is my sister: for he feared to say, She is my wife; lest, said he, the men of the place should kill me for Rebekah; because she was fair to look upon.
Leviticus 6:4

Then it shall be, because he hath sinned, and is guilty, that he shall restore that which he took violently away, or the thing which he hath deceitfully gotten, or that which was delivered him to keep, or the lost thing which he found,
Psalm 32:5
I acknowledged my sin unto thee, and mine iniquity have I not hid. I said, I will confess my transgressions unto the LORD; and thou forgavest the iniquity of my sin. Selah.
corruption_summary: Guilt is redefined as a harmful emotion to be relieved, and a generation is offered relief from a feeling while the fact that produced it goes untouched.
corruption_paragraphs: The therapeutic account of guilt treats it as a symptom: an internalized voice, a residue of upbringing, something to be worked through and dissolved. There is real pastoral use in distinguishing a scrupulous conscience from a true accusation, and Scripture does so. But the dominant modern move goes further and denies the category itself, leaving a man with nothing to do about the fact but persuade himself it is not one. Genesis 26 assumes the opposite: guilt is something that can be brought upon a people by an act, whatever anyone feels about it, and a pagan king can see it.

The biblical remedy therefore addresses the fact and reaches the feeling through it, not the other way round. The trespass offering required restitution plus a fifth and a ram; David's relief came not from reframing but from confession met by forgiveness — thou forgavest the iniquity of my sin. And the New Testament makes the offering a Person: the conscience is purged by the blood of Christ, which is the only thing in the universe that can address both the status and the sense of it. A relief that leaves the guilt in place is a cruelty with a kind face.

pos: n. (oblivion; in Psalm 88, the name given to the land of the dead)
etymology: From Old English forgietan, to forget. At Psalm 88:12 it renders Hebrew neshiyyah, oblivion — used once in Scripture, as a name for the grave.
biblical_def:
Psalm 88 is the darkest psalm in the Psalter and the only one that ends without light. Its questions come in a row, and each is rhetorical: Shall thy wonders be known in the dark? and thy righteousness in the land of forgetfulness? The Hebrew word appears nowhere else — neshiyyah, oblivion — and Heman uses it as a place-name for the grave. He is arguing with God from the grave's uselessness: the dead cannot praise, cannot testify, cannot make Your wonders known; therefore keep me here. It is a real argument, made in real desperation, and God saw fit to put it in the hymnbook.

The psalm's last line is Lover and friend hast thou put far from me, and mine acquaintance into darkness, and there it stops. No turn, no resolution. Its presence in the canon is a mercy to every believer who has been told that a Christian always comes out the other side by the end of the day. Some do not, and Scripture has a psalm for them. And the counterweight is not inside Psalm 88 but elsewhere in the same book: he knoweth our frame; he remembereth that we are dust. Heman fears a land of forgetfulness; the psalter's answer is a God who does not forget, and the New Testament makes the answer flesh — the resurrection means the land of forgetfulness has an exit, and One who has already used it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): loss of remembrance; oblivion; the state of being forgotten.
webster_full: FORGETFULNESS, n. The quality of losing the remembrance of a thing; oblivion; a ceasing to remember.
OBLIVION, n. Forgetfulness; cessation of remembrance; a state of being forgotten.
GRAVE, n. A pit or deep place in the earth; the place where a dead body is buried.

FRAME, n. The constitution or make of a thing; the form or structure of an animal body.
scriptures: Psalm 88:12
Shall thy wonders be known in the dark? and thy righteousness in the land of forgetfulness?
Psalm 88:1
O LORD God of my salvation, I have cried day and night before thee:
Psalm 88:18
Lover and friend hast thou put far from me, and mine acquaintance into darkness.
Psalm 103:14
For he knoweth our frame; he remembereth that we are dust.
corruption_summary: Psalm 88 is skipped, and believers in prolonged darkness conclude their experience has no place in Scripture — when God has given them an entire psalm that does not resolve.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 88 is almost never preached and almost never sung, and its absence teaches something false. A believer in a long darkness learns from the church's repertoire that every night ends before the benediction, and when his does not he concludes that his faith has failed. The psalm says otherwise by existing. It is a Maschil, an instructional psalm, addressed to the chief Musician for public use, and it begins by calling God the God of my salvation while describing a man whose acquaintance has been put into darkness. Faith is present in every line; relief is not.

There is no significant postmodern redefinition of this word to rebut. The principle to recover is that the canon includes this and that a congregation should say it aloud. Heman's fear was a land of forgetfulness, a place where God's wonders could not be known and His righteousness not declared, and he prayed against it day and night. The answer Scripture gives is not a happier ending to Psalm 88 but a tomb found empty on the third day, which means that oblivion is not the last address of anyone in Christ, and that the God who remembers we are dust did not leave His own Son in the dark.

pos: n. pl. (relentings; in Hosea 11:8, God's own compassions kindled together over Ephraim)
etymology: From Old French repentir, from Latin paenitere, to cause regret. At Hosea 11:8 it renders Hebrew nichum, compassion or consolation — a word of relenting mercy, not of sorrow for sin.
biblical_def:
Hosea 11 begins When Israel was a child, then I loved him, and called my son out of Egypt, and works through the whole history of a people who ran from the One who taught them to walk. Then the chapter turns, and the turn is a series of questions God asks Himself: How shall I give thee up, Ephraim? how shall I deliver thee, Israel? how shall I make thee as Admah? how shall I set thee as Zeboim? mine heart is turned within me, my repentings are kindled together. Admah and Zeboim were the cities destroyed with Sodom. The question is whether Ephraim will be given the same, and the answer comes in the next verse: I will not execute the fierceness of mine anger, I will not return to destroy Ephraim.

The reason given is the most important clause in the passage, and it guards the whole doctrine: for I am God, and not man; the Holy One in the midst of thee. The mercy is not offered as evidence that God is like us in changing His mind. It is offered as evidence that He is not like us — that where a man's patience would have run out, His does not. The Hebrew word rendered repentings is not the word for repenting of sin but for compassion, the relenting of mercy, and the verb kindled is used of warmth growing. This is God's own account of what happens in Him when He looks at a people who deserve Sodom's end.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): relentings; compassions; the meltings of pity or mercy.
webster_full: REPENTING, n. The act of repenting; relenting; the meltings of compassion.
RELENT, v.i. To soften in temper; to become more mild and tender; to feel compassion.
COMPASSION, n. A suffering with another; pity; commiseration; that disposition which is excited by the distress of another.
KINDLE, v.t. To set on fire; to inflame; to excite; to rouse; to exasperate or to warm.

scriptures: Hosea 11:8

How shall I give thee up, Ephraim? how shall I deliver thee, Israel? how shall I make thee as Admah? how shall I set thee as Zeboim? mine heart is turned within me, my repentings are kindled together.
Hosea 11:9
I will not execute the fierceness of mine anger, I will not return to destroy Ephraim: for I am God, and not man; the Holy One in the midst of thee: and I will not enter into the city.
Hosea 11:1
When Israel was a child, then I loved him, and called my son out of Egypt.
Psalm 103:14
For he knoweth our frame; he remembereth that we are dust.
corruption_summary: Hosea 11:8 is used to argue that God changes, feels as creatures feel, and does not know what He will do — when the next verse gives the reason as precisely the opposite.
corruption_paragraphs: Open Theism and process theology both reach for this verse. If God asks How shall I give thee up? and His heart is turned within Him, then surely He deliberates, is moved, and may be surprised. But verse 9 supplies the ground of the mercy and it is not that God is like us: for I am God, and not man; the Holy One in the midst of thee. The passage argues from God's unlikeness to man, not from His likeness. A man in that position would have finished Ephraim; God does not, because He is God. To read the verse as evidence of creaturely mutability is to take the sentence and drop its reason.

The confessional doctrine is that God is without body, parts or passions — impassible and immutable — and that Scripture speaks of His heart, His arm, His repenting and His relenting in the way a father speaks to children, condescending to be understood. This is not a device for explaining texts away; the Reformed tradition has always insisted that these passages tell us true things about God's disposition toward His people. What they do not tell us is that He is moved about as we are. Hosea 11 is therefore both more tender and more solid than the reading that makes God changeable: the compassions kindled there cannot cool, because the One in whom they burn does not change.

pos: n. (unrest of heart; the noise inside a man under the hand of God for his sin)
etymology: From Old French desquieter, to disturb, from Latin quietus, at rest. At Psalm 38:8 it renders Hebrew nahamah, a groaning or roaring — a word used of the growl of a lion and the roar of the sea.
biblical_def:
Psalm 38 is one of the seven penitential psalms, and David describes his condition without any attempt to look composed: I am feeble and sore broken: I have roared by reason of the disquietness of my heart. The Hebrew behind disquietness is a word for a growl or a roar, so the line is almost doubled — he roars because of the roaring within. Three verses earlier he has named the cause: mine iniquities are gone over mine head: as an heavy burden they are too heavy for me. This is not affliction from outside. It is a believer under the hand of God for his own sin, and the psalm does not pretend the two feel different from the inside.

What keeps the psalm from despair is one sentence in the middle: Lord, all my desire is before thee; and my groaning is not hid from thee. He does not have words that will do; he has a groan, and the groan is already known. The Psalter's other great treatment of the disquiet heart is the refrain of Psalms 42 and 43, where the man turns and cross-examines himself: Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted in me? hope thou in God: for I shall yet praise him for the help of his countenance. Two things are being done in these psalms — the trouble is told to God honestly, and the soul is preached to firmly — and the Christian who does only one of them will not get through.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): uneasiness; restlessness; want of tranquillity in body or mind.
webster_full: DISQUIETNESS, n. Uneasiness; restlessness; disturbance of peace in body or mind.
DISQUIET, v.t. To disturb; to deprive of peace, rest or tranquillity; to make uneasy or restless.
GROAN, n. A deep sigh uttered in distress or pain; a mournful sound.
PENITENTIAL, a. Proceeding from or expressing penitence or contrition of heart.
CONTRITE, a. Broken-hearted for sin; deeply affected with grief and sorrow for having offended God.
scriptures: Psalm 38:8
I am feeble and sore broken: I have roared by reason of the disquietness of my heart.
Psalm 38:4
For mine iniquities are gone over mine head: as an heavy burden they are too heavy for me.
Psalm 38:9
Lord, all my desire is before thee; and my groaning is not hid from thee.
Psalm 42:5
Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted in me? hope thou in God: for I shall yet praise him for the help of his countenance.
corruption_summary: Conviction of sin is diagnosed away as anxiety, or anxiety is misdiagnosed as conviction; the psalms model a man who brings the whole disturbance to God and lets Him sort it.
corruption_paragraphs: Two opposite mistakes crowd a disquieted Christian. One treats every inner disturbance as a medical or psychological matter with no moral content, so that a genuine conviction of sin is sedated. The other treats every disturbance as conviction, so that a believer whose body or circumstances are the trouble is driven to hunt for sins he has not committed. Psalm 38 belongs to the first category unmistakably — David names his iniquity as the cause — and Psalm 88 belongs to neither, since Heman names no sin at all. The Bible refuses a single diagnosis, and so should the church.

What both psalms model is the same practice: bring the whole thing to God as it is. David does not tidy up the roaring before he prays it; he says my groaning is not hid from thee, which is a statement of fact rather than a request. And the sons of Korah add the second discipline, which is preaching to oneself: hope thou in God: for I shall yet praise him. Honest complaint without self-address becomes brooding; self-address without honest complaint becomes pretence. The Psalter does both, in that order, and the man doing them is the same man.
roots_summary: Hebrew nahamah (H5100), a groaning or roaring; shaag (H7580), to roar as a lion; anachah (H584), a sighing.
roots_lines: Hebrew nahamah (H5100) — a growling, a roaring; the disquietness of the heart in Psalm 38:8.
Hebrew shaag (H7580) — to roar; the verb David uses of himself.
Hebrew anachah (H584) — a sighing, a groan; not hid from God.
Hebrew hamah (H1993) — to murmur, to be in an uproar; the disquiet of the soul in Psalm 42:5.
Hebrew yachal (H3176) — to wait, to hope; the command the psalmist gives his own soul.
usage: “I have roared by reason of the disquietness of my heart” — a roar because of a roaring.
“my groaning is not hid from thee” — stated as fact, not request.
“hope thou in God: for I shall yet praise him” — a man taking himself in hand.

pos: adj. (mournful; of the voice Darius used at the mouth of the lions' den)
etymology: From Latin lamentabilis, from lamentari, to wail. At Daniel 6:20 it renders an Aramaic word meaning grieved or pained — the king's voice after a sleepless night.
biblical_def:
Darius has been manoeuvred by his own princes into signing a decree he could not revoke, and has spent the night fasting, refusing music, unable to sleep. At first light he runs to the den: And when he came to the den, he cried with a lamentable voice unto Daniel: and the king spake and said to Daniel, O Daniel, servant of the living God, is thy God, whom thou servest continually, able to deliver thee from the lions? It is one of the most affecting moments in the Old Testament — the most powerful man in the world shouting into a pit, hoping.

Two details in the king's own words repay attention. He calls Daniel servant of the living God, a confession from a pagan monarch, and he had already said the night before, Thy God whom thou servest continually, he will deliver thee. What made Darius say that was not theology but a lifetime of watching one man's habits. Daniel's enemies had counted on the same thing — they framed the decree precisely because they knew he would pray three times a day with his windows open toward Jerusalem, and that he would not stop. And the answer that comes up out of the dark is as calm as the king's voice is not: My God hath sent his angel, and hath shut the lions' mouths.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): to be lamented; mournful; expressing sorrow; sorrowful.
webster_full: LAMENTABLE, a. To be lamented; mournful; adapted to awaken grief; expressing sorrow.
LAMENT, v.i. To mourn; to weep or wail; to express sorrow.
DEN, n. A cave or hollow place in the earth; a cavern used as a lair by wild beasts.
DECREE, n. Judicial decision, or determination of a litigated cause; an edict or law made by a superior authority.
INNOCENCY, n. Freedom from guilt; harmlessness; simplicity of heart.
scriptures: Daniel 6:20

And when he came to the den, he cried with a lamentable voice unto Daniel: and the king spake and said to Daniel, O Daniel, servant of the living God, is thy God, whom thou servest continually, able to deliver thee from the lions?
Daniel 6:16
Then the king commanded, and they brought Daniel, and cast him into the den of lions. Now the king spake and said unto Daniel, Thy God whom thou servest continually, he will deliver thee.
Daniel 6:22
My God hath sent his angel, and hath shut the lions' mouths, that they have not hurt me: forasmuch as before him innocency was found in me; and also before thee, O king, have I done no hurt.
Ecclesiastes 7:2
It is better to go to the house of mourning, than to go to the house of feasting: for that is the end of all men; and the living will lay it to his heart.
corruption_summary: Daniel 6 is filed as a children's story, and the adult point — that a law was written specifically to make faithfulness illegal, and a man kept his windows open — is lost.
corruption_paragraphs: The lions' den survives in most memories as a picture book, and the actual mechanism of the chapter is forgotten. Daniel's enemies could find no fault in his administration, so they concluded, in so many words, that they would find occasion against him concerning the law of his God. They then drafted a thirty-day statute, formally lawful, that made his ordinary devotion a capital offence. Daniel did not protest the decree, did not organize, and did not hide: he went into his house, his windows being open in his chamber toward Jerusalem, he kneeled upon his knees three times a day... as he did aforetime. The phrase as he did aforetime is the whole of it. He changed nothing.

The other half is Darius, and he is a warning to any man with authority. He was not malicious; he was flattered, hurried, and trapped by his own signature, and he spent the night paying for it. A ruler who signs what is put in front of him because it honours him will find himself shouting into a pit at daybreak. And the pagan king's lamentable voice asking whether the living God is able is answered by the quiet voice from the dark — which is how Scripture usually arranges these things.
roots_summary: Aramaic atsib (H6088), grieved, pained; gob (H1358), a den or pit; shezib (H7804), to deliver.
roots_lines: Aramaic atsib (H6088) — grieved, pained; the adjective on the king's voice.
Aramaic gob (H1358) — a den, a pit; where Daniel spent the night.
Aramaic shezib (H7804) — to rescue, to deliver; used repeatedly in the chapter of what God can do.
Aramaic chay (H2417) — living; servant of the living God, from a pagan king's mouth.
Aramaic zakku (H2136) — innocency, purity; found in Daniel before God and before the king.
usage: “he cried with a lamentable voice unto Daniel” — the most powerful man in the world, shouting into a pit.
“Thy God whom thou servest continually” — a pagan's testimony to a lifetime of habit.
“My God hath sent his angel” — the answer from the dark.

pos: n. pl. (struggles; Rachel's word for the contest with her sister that named Naphtali)
etymology: From Old English wraestlian, to wrestle. At Genesis 30:8 it renders Hebrew naphtul, a twisting or wrestling — the root of the name Naphtali, and used only here.
biblical_def:
Jacob's household is a battlefield between two sisters, and the sixth son is named for it: And Rachel said, With great wrestlings have I wrestled with my sister, and I have prevailed: and she called his name Naphtali. The Hebrew doubles the word — wrestlings of God have I wrestled — and the naming is a victory cry over a sister in a contest neither of them chose and both of them fed. Scripture records the polygamy of the patriarchs without a word of approval anywhere; what it records instead are the consequences, running through Genesis and out the far side into the sale of Joseph.

The same root gives a far greater scene two chapters later, when Jacob himself is left alone and there wrestled a man with him until the breaking of the day, and Jacob, thigh out of joint and unable to stand, says the sentence that made him Israel: I will not let thee go, except thou bless me. The New Testament carries the image into two places. Epaphras is described as always labouring fervently for you in prayers — the Greek is agonizomai, to agonize, wrestle — and Paul names the real opponent: we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world. Rachel wrestled her sister; Jacob wrestled God and lost and was blessed; the Christian is told which of the two contests is his.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): struggles; contentions; the act of striving or contending, as in a close grapple.
webster_full: WRESTLING, n. The act of striving to throw an antagonist; a struggle; a contest.
WRESTLE, v.i. To strive with arms extended, as two men, who seek to throw each other down; to struggle.
PREVAIL, v.i. To overcome; to gain the victory or superiority; to be in force.
FERVENT, a. Hot; boiling; ardent; very warm in feeling; earnest.
PRINCIPALITY, n. Sovereignty; supreme power; a prince; one invested with sovereignty.
scriptures: Genesis 30:8
And Rachel said, With great wrestlings have I wrestled with my sister, and I have prevailed: and she called his name Naphtali.
Genesis 32:24
And Jacob was left alone; and there wrestled a man with him until the breaking of the day.
Genesis 32:26
And he said, Let me go, for the day breaketh. And he said, I will not let thee go, except thou bless me.
Ephesians 6:12
For we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in high places.
corruption_summary: The patriarchs' polygamy is read as divine endorsement, when Genesis narrates it as a wound that runs the length of the book.
corruption_paragraphs: It is regularly claimed that Scripture endorses polygamy because the patriarchs practised it. Genesis does nothing of the kind. It records the practice and then records what it produced: two sisters at war, handmaids drafted into the contest, children named after grudges, a father with favourites, and eleven brothers who sold the twelfth into Egypt. The creation ordinance given before any of it was they twain shall be one flesh, and our Lord went back past Moses to that ordinance when He was asked about marriage. The narrative method of Genesis is to let the consequences preach, and on this subject they preach at length.

The other lesson is in the two kinds of wrestling the same root describes. Rachel wrestled her sister and prevailed, and the victory bought her nothing; she dies in childbirth on the road to Bethlehem a few chapters later. Jacob wrestled the Angel of the LORD, was crippled, could not prevail, and came away with a new name and a blessing. The Christian's contest, Paul says, is not with flesh and blood — not with the sister, the rival, the brother in the next pew — and a great deal of energy spent prevailing over people is energy taken from the one struggle that matters.
roots_summary: Hebrew naphtul (H5319), a wrestling; abaq (H79), to grapple in the dust; Greek pale (G3823), a wrestling; agonizomai (G75), to strive.
roots_lines: Hebrew naphtul (H5319) — a wrestling, a twisting; used once, and giving Naphtali his name.
Hebrew abaq (H79) — to grapple, from the word for dust; the verb of Jacob's night at Peniel.
Greek pale (G3823) — a wrestling, hand-to-hand struggle; Ephesians 6:12.
Greek agonizomai (G75) — to contend as in the games; Epaphras labouring fervently in prayer.
Hebrew barak (H1288) — to bless; what Jacob would not let go without.
usage: “With great wrestlings have I wrestled with my sister” — a son named after a grudge.
“I will not let thee go, except thou bless me” — the other wrestling, and the better one.
“we wrestle not against flesh and blood” — where the contest actually is.

pos: adv. (grievously, severely; of the archers who sorely grieved Joseph and could not break his bow)
etymology: From Old English sar, painful. At Genesis 49:23 it intensifies the verb of grieving — the Hebrew uses the root doubled, a form of emphasis the AV renders with the adverb.
biblical_def:
Jacob's blessing on Joseph is the longest of the twelve and the only one built entirely on a picture: The archers have sorely grieved him, and shot at him, and hated him: But his bow abode in strength, and the arms of his hands were made strong by the hands of the mighty God of Jacob; (from thence is the shepherd, the stone of Israel:). Three verbs of attack — grieved, shot, hated — and then a but that reassigns all the credit. His bow held; and the reason his bow held is that his arms were made strong by another's hands.

The archers are not identified, and they do not need to be: the brothers at the pit, Potiphar's wife, the butler who forgot him, the years in the prison. Joseph himself gave the summary of the whole business to the men who fired the first arrows: ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive. The parenthesis in Jacob's blessing is one of the loveliest in Genesis — from thence is the shepherd, the stone of Israel — two titles that would be filled out completely only in Christ. The pattern is set here: shot at, hated, held up by hands not his own, and made the means of saving much people alive.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): with violence; painfully; grievously; severely.
webster_full: SORELY, adv. With violence; painfully; grievously; severely; greatly.
SORE, a. Tender and susceptible of pain from pressure; painful; also, grievous; severe; afflictive.
ARCHER, n. A bowman; one who shoots with a bow; one who is skilful with the bow.
GRIEVE, v.t. To give pain of mind to; to afflict; to wound the feelings.
ABIDE, v.i. To rest or dwell; to continue permanently or in the same state; to remain firm or stable.
scriptures: Genesis 49:23
The archers have sorely grieved him, and shot at him, and hated him:
Genesis 49:24
But his bow abode in strength, and the arms of his hands were made strong by the hands of the mighty God of Jacob; (from thence is the shepherd, the stone of Israel:)
Psalm 38:8
I am feeble and sore broken: I have roared by reason of the disquietness of my heart.
Isaiah 23:5
As at the report concerning Egypt, so shall they be sorely pained at the report of Tyre.
corruption_summary: Endurance is credited to the man who endured, when Jacob's blessing takes even the strength of Joseph's arms and assigns it to the hands of the mighty God of Jacob.
corruption_paragraphs: Joseph is the most obvious candidate in Scripture for a story about character — wronged repeatedly, faithful throughout, vindicated at last — and that is how he is usually preached. Jacob's own blessing declines the reading. The bow abode in strength; the arms of his hands were made strong by the hands of the mighty God of Jacob. The grammar is passive, and the agent is named. Joseph did hold, and the holding was a gift. This is the ordinary Reformed way of reading any saint's perseverance: the man really perseveres, and the perseverance is God's work in him, and the two statements are not in competition.

The corresponding comfort is for anyone under sustained attack who suspects his own bow will not hold. The archers in Genesis 49 grieved Joseph sorely, and the text does not minimize it — thirteen years between the pit and the palace, most of them in a prison on a false charge. What it promises is not that the arrows will stop but that the arms will be made strong by hands other than his own. And the parenthesis points past Joseph to the One who is Himself the shepherd and the stone, who was shot at and hated and did not break, and whose holding is the reason any of His people hold.
roots_summary: Hebrew marar (H4843), to be bitter, to grieve; rabab (H7232), to shoot; eythan (H386), firm, enduring.
roots_lines: Hebrew marar (H4843) — to be bitter, to grieve; doubled in Genesis 49:23 for emphasis.
Hebrew rabab (H7232) — to shoot arrows; what the archers did.
Hebrew eythan (H386) — perennial, firm; his bow abode in strength.
Hebrew abir (H46) — mighty one; the mighty God of Jacob.
Hebrew eben (H68) — a stone; the stone of Israel, a title fulfilled in Christ.
usage: “The archers have sorely grieved him” — three verbs of attack, unminimized.
“the arms of his hands were made strong” — passive, with the agent named.
“from thence is the shepherd, the stone of Israel” — the parenthesis pointing past Joseph.
